notes.text: Word order is free in Sanskrit. The ending on each word says who did what, so poets rearrange lines at will.
Namaste is namah plus te: a bow to you. You are not saying hello, you are handing someone a bow.
Polite you is bhavaan, and it takes third person verbs. Bhavaan katham asti asks how your honour is.
Sanskrit has a dual as well as a plural. Pitarau, two fathers, is the ordinary way to say parents.
Bhojanam, a meal, comes from bhuj: to enjoy. Sanskrit files eating under pleasure, not under fuel.
Count eka, dvi, trayah and you are saying one, two, three. Shatam is a hundred, the same root as century.
Raga means colour and also passion, and later a musical mode. To be coloured by something is to love it.
Yatra covers a bus ride and a pilgrimage alike. Sanskrit never decided that going somewhere holy needed a separate word.
Hindi kal means yesterday or tomorrow. Sanskrit keeps them apart: hyah is yesterday, shvah tomorrow, adya today.
Kraya is buying. Add vi and you get vikraya, selling: one small prefix turns the whole transaction around.
Svasthya, health, breaks into sva plus stha: standing in yourself. Being well means being settled where you belong.
Grha comes from grah, to grasp. A house is what you hold, and the householder is called a grhastha.
Karma is just work or action here, no cosmic ledger. Karyam is the narrower thing: something still to be done.
Sukha and duhkha once described axle holes: a good one rides smooth, a bad one jolts. Happiness was a well-made wheel.
Utsava, a festival, is ut plus su: to lift up. The word says a festival is meant to raise people.
